transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

My family keeps telling me everything is normal, but I’m absolutely convinced they’re secretly working together behind my back. I just can't shake this belief, no matter what papers or proof they try to show me. It is incredibly frustrating because they all act like I'm just imagining things.
How long have you been holding this belief about your family?

It’s been going on for about eleven months now. It all started when we had to deal with the sale of my parents' old house and sorting out all their papers. Ever since those arguments started, I've known they were working behind my back.
Aside from these concerns about your family, have you heard any voices or seen things that other people don't seem to notice?
No, nothing like that at all. I haven't heard any unusual voices or seen anything out of the ordinary. My mind is perfectly clear, and my only concern is what my family is doing behind my back.
During these past eleven months, have you also been feeling consistently down, depressed, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?
No, I haven't really felt down or lost interest in my usual activities at all. My main distress and focus are entirely on this situation with my family and the plotting they are doing behind my back.
Apart from the stress caused by this situation with your family, are you still able to manage your daily routine, work, and other relationships as you normally would?

Yes, I still manage my office team perfectly fine and keep up all my volunteer shifts at the senior center without any issues. However, my family life is a mess—I've completely stopped going to family gatherings because they are just too tense and exhausting, always ending in arguments about what they are planning behind my back.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (believing family members are plotting behind their back) lasting for 11 months. Other psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations, are absent, and there is no evidence of a mood disorder. Outside of the specific delusional theme and its impact on family relationships, the patient's psychosocial and occupational functioning is well-preserved, which strongly supports the diagnosis of Delusional Disorder (F22.0) over Schizophrenia (F20.0).
